introduction_markdown: Multiple choice paper (English Language 1, June 2026, Ordinary Level, code 0530). Answer ALL 50 questions; all questions carry equal marks. Each question has four suggested answers A, B, C and D; mark only one answer for each question. The paper has four sections: A listening comprehension (questions 1-10), B reading comprehension (questions 11-25), C grammar (questions 26-40) and D vocabulary (questions 41-50).
enonce_intro_markdown: **Multiple choice questions** - choose the one correct answer, A, B, C or D.
incertitudes: Questions 8, 13, 17, 23, 26, 37, 40 et 47 : clé non établie avec certitude ou option fautive, donc ingérées comme questions OUVERTES (auto-évaluation). Q8 : le sujet impose EITHER (accentuation, clé B again) OR (sens, clé D) sous un seul numéro, donc pas de clé unique. Q13 : A afraid of contre B cautious of. Q17 : D caution contre B advice. Q23 : D jovial contre C loud. Q26 : l'option A est imprimée fautive ("will have wither") ; B will wither est aussi défendable. Q37 : C the/the contre A an/the. Q40 : aucune version imprimée n'est entièrement correcte, C est la plus proche. Q47 : aucune option n'est un synonyme de leaked, B sold est la plus proche.
Question 5 : clé B (to entertain himself) ; concurrente A (he was bored), l'ennui étant la cause et le divertissement le but énoncé.
Question 7 : clé D (the boy had lied to them again) ; concurrente A (the boy cried).
Question 25 : clé D (satisfaction) ; le texte ne l'énonce pas, c'est le ton le plus cohérent avec la fin du récit.
Question 36 : clé C (never to disrespect her parents) ; concurrente B (to never ..., infinitif séparé).
Question 39 : clé B (is, accord avec driver, seul singulier proposé) ; l'usage courant pourrait faire retenir A (were).
Question 50 : clé C (come after) ; concurrente A (follow behind).
Questions 19, 20 et 22 : clés B, A et A déduites du récit (le texte ne donne pas de formulation explicite).
Le sujet imprime "The active form of the expression ' He was made to confess by the police" (guillemet ouvrant sans fermant, souligné) à la question 35 : reprise telle quelle.

Les mots soulignés des questions 47 à 50 sont rendus en gras, faute de souligné fiable en Markdown. Les numéros de ligne du passage de lecture sont repris entre crochets, à la fin de la ligne imprimée ; les renvois du sujet (lignes 22, 30, 52, 55) ne correspondent pas toujours exactement à la numérotation imprimée.

Le texte de l'écoute (Section A) vient des pages d'instructions du professeur, recopié sans les barres obliques de pause ; le tiret cadratin devant "even if you're telling the truth" est remplacé par un tiret simple. Les titres Section One/Two/Three du livret correspondent aux questions 1-4, 5-7 et 8-10.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**Listening passage (read aloud once by the examiner in the real exam - read it once, then answer)**

**Lying**

**Section 1**

Throughout the years, lying has had a huge amount of power. Lying has changed, and so has the way people lie, but the reason for lying hasn't. People lie out of fear, revenge, sadness, or selfishness. Lying can also take the form of a disease, as some people can eventually become permanent liars, as they constantly lie, even if it serves no special purpose. Such persons have become addicted to lying. Even though we sometimes lie to save a situation, we must also be very careful about the frequency of the act of lying we resort to. Remember especially that, lying breaks trust - even if you're telling the truth, no one believes a liar. Once your friends and family consider you a liar even when you tell the truth no one will believe you. Listen to what happened to a young man who was grazing cattle.

**Section 2**

Once, there was a boy who became bored when he watched over the village sheep grazing on the hillside. To entertain himself, he cried out, "Wolf! Wolf! The wolf is chasing the sheep!"

When the villagers heard the cry, they came running up the hill to drive the wolf away. But, when they arrived, they saw no wolf. The boy was amused when he saw their angry faces.

"Don't scream wolf, boy," warned the villagers, "when there is no wolf!" They angrily went back down the hill.

Later, the shepherd boy cried out once again, "Wolf! Wolf! The wolf is chasing the sheep!" To his amusement, he looked on as the villagers came running up the hill to scare the wolf away.

As they saw there was no wolf, they said once more seriously, "Save your frightened cry for when there really is a wolf! Don't cry 'wolf' when there is no wolf!" But the boy grinned at their words while they walked away grumbling down the hill once more.

**Section 3**

Later, the boy saw a real wolf sneaking around his flock. Alarmed, he jumped on his feet and cried out as loud as he could, "Wolf! Wolf!" But the villagers thought he was fooling them again, and so they didn't come to help.

At sunset, the villagers went looking for the boy who hadn't returned with their sheep. When they went up the hill, they found him bleeding profusely and also weeping.

"There really was a wolf here! The flock is gone! I cried out, 'Wolf!' but you didn't come," he wailed.

An old man went to comfort the boy. As he put his arm around him while cleaning his wounds, he said, "Nobody believes a liar, even when he is telling the truth!"

**Section A - Listening comprehension (5 marks).** Choose the best answer from the alternatives (A, B, C and D) for each of the questions below. Using only the material read to you from the listening comprehension passage, answer each question as directed.

**Section One**

1. People lie out of \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The speaker says "People lie out of fear, revenge, sadness, or selfishness". Poverty, power and trust are not given as reasons. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Listening passage above) Section One

2. Lying can be a disease when one lies \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The passage says lying can take the form of a disease when people "constantly lie, even if it serves no special purpose". The reason stated is that the lying serves no special purpose. "All the time" describes how often, not the condition the passage names. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Listening passage above) Section One

3. According to the passage, one could sometimes lie \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The speaker says "Even though we sometimes lie to save a situation". Punishment and favour are not mentioned. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Listening passage above) Section One

4. The expression, "lying breaks trust" suggests that \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The sentence continues "even if you're telling the truth, no one believes a liar": once trust is broken, nobody believes you. Addiction is mentioned elsewhere in the passage, and dislike is never stated. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: family members consider you as a liar

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Listening passage above) Section Two

5. In this passage, the boy cried 'wolf' because \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The passage says the boy became bored, and then "To entertain himself, he cried out". Boredom is the state that led to it, but the stated purpose of the cry is to entertain himself. The wolf was not really chasing the sheep (that was the lie). **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: the wolf was chasing the sheep

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Listening passage above) Section Two

6. The word 'amused' read to you from the passage means \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: "The boy was amused when he saw their angry faces": he found it funny and was pleased. "Amused" is closest to "happy"; "bored" is the earlier state, and the boy was neither amazed nor encouraged by the villagers. **Answer: A.**
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Listening passage above) Section Two

7. The villagers angrily walked down the hill because \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: They found no wolf: the boy had made them climb the hill for nothing and had lied to them again. The cry itself (A) is why they came up, not why they were angry. They were not afraid, and the wolf never existed in the false alarms. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: the boy had lied to them again

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Listening passage above) Section Three

8. **EITHER** You have heard the word "returned" read to you from the passage. Tick the word below with the stress pattern as in "returned".

*Options as printed:* A) bleeding B) again C) normal D) pleasant

**OR** The boy did not return with the sheep because \_\_\_\_\_\_.

*Options as printed:* A) he was fooling the villagers B) he was seriously wounded C) the villager didn't come to help D) a wolf had attacked the flock
questions.corrige_markdown:
The printed question offers two alternatives under one number (EITHER ... OR), so it cannot carry a single key and is left open for self-assessment.

**EITHER (stress):** "returned" is stressed on the second syllable: reTURNED. Stress of the options: BLEEDing (first), aGAIN (second), NORmal (first), PLEASant (first). Only "again" matches. **Answer: B (again).**

**OR (meaning):** the boy had no sheep to bring back because the real wolf had attacked and scattered the flock ("The flock is gone!"). Being wounded (B) is a result of the attack, and the villagers' failure to help (C) is not the reason the sheep were missing. **Answer: D (a wolf had attacked the flock).**

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Listening passage above) Section Three

9. The villagers met him bleeding and weeping. This suggests that \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The boy was found bleeding and weeping and said "There really was a wolf here!". The injuries and tears show that a wolf really attacked him. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Listening passage above) Section Three

10. The lesson derived from this story is that \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The old man concludes "Nobody believes a liar, even when he is telling the truth": the boy lost his whole flock because of his earlier lies. The lesson is that lying can be costly. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: we should cry when there is trouble
we should be honest cattle grazers

questions.enonce_markdown:
**Section B - Reading comprehension (7½ marks).** Read the following passage and answer the questions which follow.

**Passage for questions 11 to 25** (the numbers in square brackets are the line numbers printed in the paper)

**My journey home**

When I did not hear from my father for so long, which was abnormal, I decided to send him a letter. Several weeks after sending this letter to my father, I still did not receive a reply. I sent him an express mail. Again, no response. I concluded that something must be wrong at home; perhaps with my grandmother, who had recently suffered a serious illness and virtually lost her sight. [5]

I asked the editor of my newspaper organ for a week off. The next morning I boarded a taxi to the bus station and joined several other passengers on board a station wagon bound for my home town. My mood was nostalgic throughout the seven-hour journey. Memories of my grandmother first came to mind.

My father's mother, Nne, also gave me cause for uneasiness when she foretold that I [10] would achieve success and fame only if I washed my eyes in water, and if I were wise enough to avoid the misfortunes fate would put on my path. So, my father had told me many stories of her quirky wisdom, her habit of surprising people by divining their innermost thoughts, or their dreams, or foretelling events exactly as they would happen. The day her husband died she had begged him not to climb a particular palm tree from which he would have the fatal fall. [15]

"Why are you speaking like a drunk this early in the day?" her husband had asked. The years he had lived with her had bred in him, not respect for her clairvoyance, but dismissive contempt.

"I saw in my dream a thing so terrible my mouth cannot speak about. That tree is bitter. You must sacrifice a cockerel to appease its anger". [20]

Her husband laughed her off. **"If that tree wants to eat a chicken, it must go to the market and buy itself one"**, he said. One of his customers had ordered seven gourds of palm wine for a marriage ceremony, and my grandfather was not the kind of tapper to promise seven gourds without delivery.

When he set out that morning for his tapping rounds she followed him part of the way, [25] admonishing in proverbs.

"The death that kills a puppy first blinds him. The headstrong who won't listen will finally obey the summons of the death mat. The housefly that has nobody to advise it follows the corpse into the grave". Her husband swaggered on in silence.

Later that day, an old man returning from his farm heard **muffled** groans. As he [30] followed the direction of the sound, he discovered my grandfather in a heap, blood surging from his mouth, dripping from his nostrils and seeping from his ears. The farmer ran to the village with a speed indifferent to the weariness of old bones. But when the first persons arrived at the scene, my grandfather was already dead. From this story, we learnt to listen to grandma's words with a lot of caution. [35]

Still in the car, memories of my father also floated in and out of my mind. I recalled how he had set off my romance with words, how he had taught me words and sounds long before I knew their meaning. Words that were magical music to my ears.

The car arrived late in the afternoon. I completed my journey in a cab that ran the thirty- [40] minute shuttle to my village. The driver dropped me off outside the bar in which years earlier I had listened to familiar music and conversation. Walking towards my home, I saw a woman sitting on a wooden ledge in the village square, head lifted to the sky. She called out my name. I startled, then recognized my grandmother.

"Nne," I addressed her. "What are you doing here?" [45]

**"Watching the sun go home,"** she answered.

"Watching the sun! Didn't father say ..." I squelched the indelicate question.

"That I had gone blind? Why should weakness of sight stop me escorting the journeying sun?".

"I was surprised that you called out my name. How did you know it was me?" [50]

"The scent of your spirit".

"Scent? How does my spirit smell?"

**She laughed, a high, full-hearted laughter.**

"Just like your father's; a good smell".

As we made our way home she said, "Your father is waiting for you" [55]

"Waiting? But he doesn't know I'm coming". She laughed again. "My son, you and your father carry the same blood in your bodies. He knows you are coming".

**Questions 11 to 25**

11. The narrator \_\_\_\_\_\_ communicated with his father.
questions.corrige_markdown: The narrator "did not hear from my father for so long, which was abnormal": the silence was abnormal, so they normally communicated often, i.e. usually. "Never" and "seldom" would not make the silence abnormal, and "seldomly" is not standard English. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 11 to 25 above) 12. The narrator imagined that something might be wrong with the grandmother because she \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The passage says she "had recently suffered a serious illness and virtually lost her sight". The key words are recently and serious illness. "Always" contradicts "recently", and "had suffered" omits the point. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 11 to 25 above) 13. Grandma's predictions caused the narrator to be \_\_\_\_\_\_ her.

*Options as printed:* A) afraid of B) cautious of C) careful with D) honest with
questions.corrige_markdown: Left open for self-assessment. The passage says Nne "gave me cause for uneasiness" with her predictions, which points to "afraid of" (A), but the narrator also says we learnt "to listen to grandma's words with a lot of caution", which points to "cautious of" (B). Both can be defended and "cautious of her" is an unusual collocation, so no single key is certain. "Careful with" and "honest with" do not fit. **Answer: A (afraid of) is the more natural fit for "uneasiness"; B (cautious of) is the alternative.**
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 11 to 25 above) 14. The grandmother had a special gift of \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: She was known for "foretelling events exactly as they would happen" and for divining people's thoughts and dreams. Her special gift was foretelling the future. Surprising people was only the effect. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 11 to 25 above) 15. His grandfather, in dismissing the grandmother's advice, shows that he was \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: He laughed her off and showed "dismissive contempt" for her clairvoyance: he did not believe her. Superstitious is the opposite (believing in such signs). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 11 to 25 above) 16. The expression "if that tree wants to eat a chicken, it must go to the market and buy itself one" (line 22) is \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The grandfather mocks her warning by saying the tree can buy its own chicken: a joke made to ridicule her request. Mocking remarks of this kind are sarcastic. "Ironic" is a close second, but the purpose here is to mock. **Answer: B.**
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 11 to 25 above) 17. The three proverbs altered by the tapper's wife suggest a/an \_\_\_\_\_\_.

*Options as printed:* A) ill omen B) advice C) threat D) caution
questions.corrige_markdown: Left open for self-assessment. She followed him "admonishing in proverbs": the proverbs warn the headstrong who will not listen. Both "caution" (D, a warning) and "advice" (B, the proverb says the fly "has nobody to advise it") fit, and the passage later speaks of listening to her words "with caution". An omen (A) is a sign of bad luck, not a spoken warning, and she makes no threat (C). **Answer: D (caution) is the more likely key; B (advice) is the alternative.**
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 11 to 25 above) 18. The word 'muffled' in the phrase "muffled groans" (line 30) is used as a/an \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: "Muffled" describes the noun "groans", so it is an adjective (a past participle used as an adjective). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 11 to 25 above) 19. The narrator's grandfather must have died because he had \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The grandmother had begged him not to climb the palm tree "from which he would have the fatal fall"; he was then found in a heap, bleeding, after his tapping rounds. He died of a fall from the palm tree. "Wounded" is too vague and does not name the cause. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: taken a lot of palm wine

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 11 to 25 above) 20. In teaching the child, the narrator's father can be described as \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The father "taught me words and sounds long before I knew their meaning" and set off the narrator's romance with words: a gentle, loving way of teaching. Nothing suggests strictness or authority. **Answer: A.**
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 11 to 25 above) 21. The expression "watching the sun go home" (line 52) suggests it was \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The sun "going home" means setting, which happens at dusk (the narrator arrived late in the afternoon). **Answer: D.**
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 11 to 25 above) 22. The narrator withdrew from completing his question about grandma's sight to avoid \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: He "squelched the indelicate question": asking a blind person about her sight would have embarrassed her (and him). Disrespect is a possible reading, but the passage stresses the awkwardness of the question. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 11 to 25 above) 23. The expression "she laughed a high, full-hearted laughter" (line 55) means the laughter was \_\_\_\_\_\_.

*Options as printed:* A) passionate B) provocative C) loud D) jovial
questions.corrige_markdown: Left open for self-assessment. "High" suggests a loud, ringing laugh (C), while "full-hearted" suggests a hearty, cheerful laugh (D, jovial). Both are defensible and the passage gives no further hint. Passionate and provocative do not fit a cheerful laugh. **Answer: D (jovial) captures the mood of the scene; C (loud) is the alternative.**
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 11 to 25 above) 24. This story covers \_\_\_\_\_\_ generations.
questions.corrige_markdown: The story involves the narrator's grandparents (first generation), his father (second generation) and the narrator himself (third generation). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 11 to 25 above) 25. The general feeling at the end of the story is that of \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The story ends warmly: the grandmother is calm and laughing, she says "a good smell", and she affirms that the father knows the narrator is coming. The mood is one of satisfaction and reassurance, not fear, doubt or sorrow. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
**Section C - Grammar (7½ marks).** For numbers 26-40 choose the best answer that completes each sentence.

26. By the time it rains, my flowers \_\_\_\_\_\_.

*Options as printed:* A) will have wither B) will wither C) would have withered D) have withered
questions.corrige_markdown: Left open for self-assessment because option A is misprinted ("will have wither" instead of "will have withered"). "By the time" with a present tense verb in the time clause calls for the future perfect in the main clause: "will have withered", so A is the intended key. "Will wither" (B) is also grammatical in some contexts, "would have withered" is a past-unreal form and "have withered" ignores the future. **Answer: A (intended: "will have withered"), but the printed form is faulty.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 27. My neighbours aren't at home. They \_\_\_\_\_\_ out.
questions.corrige_markdown: The neighbours are not at home now, so they left earlier and the result is present: the present perfect "have gone". "Are going", "shall go" and "will go" refer to the future or to an action in progress. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 28. Wisdom is said to be the application of knowledge. Wisdom and knowledge are \_\_\_\_\_\_ nouns.
questions.corrige_markdown: Wisdom and knowledge are ideas that cannot be seen or touched: abstract nouns. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 29. You and \_\_\_\_\_\_ will succeed in the coming examination.
questions.corrige_markdown: The blank is part of the compound subject of "will succeed", so the subject pronoun "I" is required. "Me" and "us" are object forms, and "they" does not fit the meaning of "you and ___". **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 30. It is \_\_\_\_\_\_ to propose an idea than to defend it.
questions.corrige_markdown: The sentence uses "than", so it needs the comparative "easier". The other options double the comparative or use a superlative. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 31. Jerry \_\_\_\_\_\_ sleeps in the afternoon. He considers it a waste of time
questions.corrige_markdown: He thinks sleeping in the afternoon is a waste of time, so he never does it. The other adverbs say that he does sleep. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 32. I have been working in town \_\_\_\_\_\_ the beginning of my career.
questions.corrige_markdown: The present perfect continuous ("have been working") takes "since" with a starting point in time. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 33. It was a rainy day \_\_\_\_\_\_ many students came late.
questions.corrige_markdown: The rain is the cause and the late arrival the result, so the result connector "so" is needed. "Since" and "because" would introduce the cause, which is the first clause. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 34. Nobody has eaten to their fill, \_\_\_\_\_\_?
questions.corrige_markdown: The main clause is negative in meaning ("nobody"), so the tag is positive; "nobody" is referred to with plural "they": "have they?". **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 35. The active form of the expression ' He was made to confess by the police is \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: In the active form the doer (the police) becomes the subject; after the active "made" the infinitive loses "to": "The police made him confess". C keeps "to", which is wrong in the active. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: The police made him to confess
The confession to the police was made by him

questions.enonce_markdown: 36. 'Never disrespect your parents', Emma told the sister. Emma advised her sister \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: A negative command is reported with an infinitive, and "your" changes to "her": "never to disrespect her parents". A and D keep "your", and D has no infinitive. B ("to never" is a split infinitive) is accepted by some writers, but C is the standard form expected in school grammar. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
37. As the president of \_\_\_\_\_\_ association, I have \_\_\_\_\_\_ obligation to follow the rules binding members.

*Options as printed:* A) an/the B) the/this C) the/the D) the/that
questions.corrige_markdown: Left open for self-assessment. "As the president of the association, I have the obligation to follow the rules" (C) is natural. But "As the president of an association, I have the obligation..." (A) is also grammatical, and "this/that obligation" is unusual because the obligation has not been mentioned before. **Answer: C (the/the) is the most natural; A (an/the) is the alternative.**
themes: O Level English - articles and determiners

questions.enonce_markdown: 38. The teacher asked you and \_\_\_\_\_\_ to clean the class.
questions.corrige_markdown: The blank is an object of "asked" together with "you", so the object pronoun "me" is needed ("The teacher asked me"). Using "I" is a common error, and "myself" has no subject to reflect. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 39. Neither the passengers nor the driver \_\_\_\_\_\_ late.
questions.corrige_markdown: With "neither ... nor" the verb agrees with the noun nearest to it, "the driver" (singular), so a singular verb is needed: "is". Among the options "is" is the only singular form ("was" is not offered). "Were" and "are" agree with the plural "passengers". **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
40. Which sentence is correctly punctuated?

*Options as printed:*

A) The master asked, who came late this morning?

B) The master asked, "who came late this morning"

C) The master asked, "who came late this morning?"

D) The master asked 'who came late this morning?
questions.corrige_markdown: Left open for self-assessment because none of the printed sentences is fully correct. The standard form is: The master asked, "Who came late this morning?" (direct speech: comma, opening quotation mark, capital W, question mark inside the quotation marks) or, as indirect speech, "The master asked who came late this morning." A mixes a comma with a question that is not direct speech, B has no question mark and no capital, D has no comma and an unclosed single quotation mark. C is the closest to correct: it has the comma, the quotation marks and the question mark inside, and lacks only the capital letter. **Answer: C is the closest to correct.**
themes: O Level English - spelling and punctuation

questions.enonce_markdown:
**Section D - Vocabulary (5 marks).** For numbers 41-46 choose the answer that best completes each sentence.

41. Mary and Susan \_\_\_\_\_\_ the floor of our house.
questions.corrige_markdown: To clean a floor with a wet mop is "to mop". "Dry-cleaned" is for clothes, "kept clean" does not take a direct action, and "mobbed" means crowded around. **Answer: C.**
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: 42. Amina stayed back to \_\_\_\_\_\_ corn for the evening meal.
questions.corrige_markdown: To thresh corn is to beat it to separate the grains before cooking. Scratch and crash do not fit, and "remove" is too general. **Answer: D.**
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: 43. In order to carry out the necessary examination, the dead body was \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: A body that is dug up from a grave for examination is "exhumed". "Extracted" is used for teeth or minerals, "exported" for goods, and "expelled" for people or air. **Answer: C.**
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: 44. The government has \_\_\_\_\_\_ smoking in public places.
questions.corrige_markdown: "Ban smoking" is the collocation: to forbid it officially. "Prevented" would need "from", and "adjusted" and "avoided" do not fit the meaning. **Answer: B.**
themes: O Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: 45. There are more than three hundred indigen\_\_\_\_\_\_ languages in Cameroon.
questions.corrige_markdown: The adjective is "indigenous" (indigen + ous). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 46. Our friend told us his father gave him 'chicken feed' for his allowance. This means his father gave him \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: "Chicken feed" is an idiom for a very small amount of money. **Answer: A.**
themes: O Level English - idioms and proverbs

choix.texte: a very small amount of money

questions.enonce_markdown:
**For numbers 47 and 48 choose the answer that best explains the meaning of the underlined word or phrase.** (Underlined words are shown in bold below.)

47. The company wanted to keep the story a secret but someone **leaked** it out to the press.

*Options as printed:* A) bought B) sold C) brought D) borrowed
questions.corrige_markdown: Left open for self-assessment because none of the printed options is a synonym of "leaked" (which means revealed or disclosed secretly). Bought, brought and borrowed do not fit at all; "sold" is the only option that can be linked to passing a secret to the press, so it is the nearest, but it is not a true synonym. **Answer: no correct synonym is printed; B (sold) is the nearest.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 48. The victim could not **identify** the thief.
questions.corrige_markdown: To identify a person is to recognise who he or she is. Discover and find mean to come across something, and "know" is a state, not an act of picking someone out. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
**For numbers 49 and 50 choose the answer that gives the opposite of the underlined word.** (Underlined words are shown in bold below.)

49. The Judge was **subjective** in his judgement.
questions.corrige_markdown: "Subjective" means influenced by personal feelings; its opposite is impartial (objective, unbiased). "Unjust" and "crooked" are not antonyms of subjective, and "correct" is not its opposite. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 50. The English Language lessons always **precede** sports and physical education lessons.
questions.corrige_markdown: "Precede" means come before, so its opposite is "come after". "Come before" is a synonym and "come along side" means come together. "Follow behind" (A) also means to come after but suggests physical movement, so C is the cleaner antonym. **Answer: C.**
